old_caveat_statements: A mistake in Eq. 1 of Ylilammi et al. (2018) was corrected by multiplying both terms on the right side by Avogadro's number.
The interaction volume of 5 kV X-rays exceeded the film thickness, causing substrate Si signal across the line scan.
Variations in chamber pressure, reflectometry measurement, and actual channel height relative to design values are major sources of uncertainty.
Measured film thickness varied by some nanometers depending on the reference measurement.
Small deviations in reactant dose can occur initially when opening a fresh precursor cylinder.
Only one specimen per condition was measured for electrical resistivity, and sensitivity to cracking or contamination requires cautious interpretation.
Reported delta n_s and delta n_g represent combined amounts across two compacts in each run, not individual specimen statistics.
Ideal exposure calculations assume unit sticking probability and therefore serve only as lower bounds for actual exposures.
The 43 L upper limit is constrained by the microbalance sensor dimensions, and the actual saturation exposure lies between 3 and 43 L.
Reactor-scale diffusion and convection increase the required exposure time above the local theoretical limit.
An approximate analytical model for reactant partial pressure is adopted to avoid computationally intensive numerical solutions during fitting.
Eq. (31) is solved numerically using the 4th order Runge-Kutta method because direct analytical integration is too slow.
Spectroscopic reflectometry thickness precision is limited by channel surface roughness to approximately 3 nm.
Diffusion of the metal precursor is assumed to be the growth-limiting factor because water molecules are smaller and diffuse much faster.
Concentration gradients in the y and z directions are assumed negligible due to fast equilibration across the gap height and a very wide lateral channel.
Reflectometer reliability degrades at film thicknesses around 10 nm, limiting accurate profiling of the ending tail.
ALD reactions are generally not at equilibrium during adsorption.
The model assumes channel height decreases uniformly each cycle by twice gpc_sat rather than using the local thickness.
Initial partial pressure of Reactant A was assumed zero along the microchannel at t = 0.
Model B equations were solved assuming free molecular flow (effective diffusion equals Knudsen diffusion) using MATLAB pdepe.
Model B used zero initial partial pressure and coverage, with fixed entrance pressure and reactive flux boundary conditions.
Half-thickness penetration depth and front slope were linearly interpolated between two adjacent discretization points.
Discretization spacing was selected to keep the difference between the two points below 1% of the y-axis range.
Molecular diffusion is assumed negligible relative to Knudsen diffusion because pore dimensions are much smaller than the mean free path.
The simulation baseline parameters represent generic values inspired by TMA-water rather than a specific real system.
XPS cannot detect hydrogen contamination, and N 1s analysis is hindered by overlap with Ga-Auger peaks.
The diffraction peak marked with an asterisk originates from the silicon substrate rather than the deposited film.
The 762-792 nm region was excluded from integrated count calculations because intense emission at 777 nm saturated the detector at higher flows and powers.
Atomic oxygen could not be reliably measured with the EQP tool due to poor signal-to-noise ratio and high background dissociation in RGA and TIMS modes.
Only qualitative conclusions are drawn from OES since Ar actinometry was not used to avoid modifying plasma and film properties.
Recombination coefficient was kept constant because the diffusion-limited experimental data were not well suited to fit it.
Plasma geometry and excitation frequency affect species delivery and temperature through wall recombination and field lines.
At lower pressures, RF power could not exceed 250 W.
